# Chapter 2 — The Mirror and the Authority

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
The obvious objection is that the enterprise already has a Git host, so why
stand up a Windows server. This chapter separates two roles the boundary will
not let one system play: the *mirror* where canon is ingested, and the
*authority* where canon is decided. It shows why GCC-Moderate forces the
authority of record inside the boundary, and how the relationship inverts so
the public host flows in while authority never flows out.
:::

## The Obvious Objection

The objection arrives immediately. The enterprise already has a Git host. It
is reliable, it is familiar, it is somebody else's operational problem, and
the canon already lives on it today. Why stand up a Windows server to do what
a SaaS platform does better and cheaper? The objection is reasonable, and the
answer is not that the SaaS platform is bad. The answer is that a mirror and
an authority are different roles, and the boundary does not let the same
system play both.

## Two Roles, One Boundary

A mirror is where canon is ingested. An authority is where canon is decided.
The distinction is not cosmetic — it determines which constraints the system
inherits.

| | **Mirror (public Git)** | **Authority (on-premises)** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Role | Ingest, collaborate, read, propose | Decide what becomes binding canon |
| Power over governance | None — it reflects | Total — the rest of the substrate obeys it |
| Boundary requirement | Convenience; may sit outside | Must sit inside GCC-Moderate |
| Inbound from internet | Permitted | None |

## The Boundary Does Not Bend

The cloud boundary for the program is GCC-Moderate, and the discipline of a
boundary is that it does not bend for convenience. Every commit, every
webhook, every audit record produced by the authority of record must sit
under the same authorization plane that governs the rest of the substrate. If
the directory, the policy engine, and the telemetry pipeline all live inside
the boundary, then the system that decides what those things *are* cannot
live outside it.

> Otherwise the most consequential object in the architecture — the one that
> defines every other object — would be governed by a different authority than
> the things it governs. That is not a tidy exception; it is a hole straight
> through the center of the model.

## The Relationship Inverts

So the relationship inverts cleanly. The public host upstream is the source
of canon *ingest*: a pull-mirror keeps the on-premises instance current with
the wider world on a short interval, and contributors who live outside the
boundary still have a place to work. The on-premises instance is the source
of canon *authority*: it is the one whose history is binding, whose hooks are
enforced, whose audit log an assessor will eventually read. The mirror flows
in; authority does not flow out.

Having established *that* the authority must live inside, the next question is
*how many* of it there should be — and the answer is more pointed than it
first appears.
